newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian officials plan Wednesday meet on Mir woes.
newsitem.headline: Russian officials plan Wednesday meet on Mir woes.

text.p: Senior Russian space officials are expected to meet on Wednesday to revise plans to repair the crippled space station after doctors told Mir's commander to begin taking pills for a heart condition.

The crew of two Russians and one British-American had been expected to undertake repairs later this week following the June 25 crash between Mir and its unmanned cargo vessel, the worst accident in its history.

But Mission Control doctor Igor Goncharov on Tuesday told commander Vasily Tsibliyev, 43, he needed to take it easy and take medication following the discovery of a slight irregularity in his heartbeat.
"He can work but we don't recommend big physical exertion," Goncharov told reporters at Mission Control outside Moscow.

The news opened up the possibility that NASA physicist Michael Foale would step in to help flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin during the risky repair operation, which seeks to restore power from solar panels damaged during the accident.
NASA officials also said they would question whether it might be better to delay repairs until after a three-man Russian-French relief crew arrives on August 7.

Tsibliyev's heart condition, which doctors said may be stress-related, was the latest in a series of setbacks the 11-year-old orbiting Mir has suffered since February when the former Soviet air force pilot came aboard.

In February, cosmonauts were forced to don gas masks after a serious fire on board that lasted 14 minutes. Then in April the crew spent weeks trying to plug holes in the station's cooling system, causing irritation from the vapour and temperatures as high as 34 degrees Celsius (96 degrees Fahrenheit).

"You feel like all you're doing is trying to stay alive," a U.S. astronaut told Reuters following a four-month stay that spanned those two crises. "You say to yourself 'what are we accomplishing here other than just existing?'"

After the June 25 accident, the Russian media blamed Tsibliyev, a veteran of a half-year Mir mission in 1993, for causing the crash by failing to reprogramme his controls to take account of waste being carried by the cargo craft he was manoeuvring.
An official investigation into whether man or machine is to blame is underway.

During a 10 a.m. (0600 GMT) meeting on Wednesday morning, senior Russian experts from the agency that designed Mir as well as rocket engineers and space agency officials were expected to plan the next steps in the repairs which include reattaching 17 cables to the solar panels in the punctured Spektr module.
Cosmonauts will have to wear bulky spacesuits in a cramped area of the sealed-off module to perform the operation which is vital for the future of the ageing space station.

A NASA official at Mission Control said Americans would need a day or two or even longer before being able to give Foale the go-ahead to lend a hand. He had originally been expected to sit in the Soyuz escape module during the work.
"The decision has not yet been made and will probably not be made for at least 24-48 hours, possibly longer," NASA official Philip Engelauf said on Tuesday. "We're just going to take our time."
